title: atlas-server & bibex — the HTTP API and the offline CLI over one graph

overview.l1: This is the front door to the whole Bible atlas. atlas-server is a small web server: it loads the one compiled graph file, then answers questions like "give me John chapter 3" or "what places does this event touch" over the network as JSON, which is what the map and reader in your browser actually talk to. atlas-cli builds the exact same questions and answers into a command-line program called bibex — think of it as the app without the browser: you type `bibex verse GEN.1.1` in a terminal and get the verse, its cross references, and everything attached to it, with no server and no network involved. If atlas-server vanished, the client would have nothing to fetch from; if atlas-cli vanished, you'd lose a fast, scriptable way to poke at the graph directly.
overview.l2: atlas-server is an axum web application. `main.rs` parses command-line flags and starts it; `load.rs` is the single function both the real binary and the test harness call to turn a data directory into a running app, so the two can never quietly diverge; `app.rs` wires every URL path to its handler function; `handlers.rs` and `graph_handlers.rs` contain those handler functions, which read query parameters, ask the graph a question through a trait called `GraphQuery`, and wrap the answer in `Json(...)`; `graph_wire.rs` converts the graph's internal ids into human-readable strings like `"Event:ab_ur"` and back. atlas-cli mirrors this shape without any of the HTTP machinery: `main.rs` hand-parses `argv`, `load.rs` loads the same compiled graph file, and each file under `commands/` is one subcommand (`verse`, `chapter`, `node`, `edges`, `find`, `kinds`, `tutorial`, `help`), each offering both a plain-text and a `--json` rendering of the identical underlying query. Both crates depend on `atlas-graph` (the query engine) and `atlas-graph-types` (the trait and id vocabulary) rather than inventing their own.
overview.l3: atlas-server exposes 22 routes off one `axum::Router` (`app.rs::build_with_sources`), backed by `AppState { data: Arc<AtlasData>, graph: Arc<GraphService>, sources: Arc<SourcesDocument> }` via `FromRef`. Every handler is `async fn(State<...>, ...) -> Result<Json<T>, ApiError>`; `ApiError` (error.rs) is the one error type, rendered as `{"error":{"code","message"}}`. The load path is deliberately singular: `load.rs::load_from_data_dir`/`load_graph_and_data` is called by both `main.rs` and `tests/contract_pact.rs`'s pact recorder, closing a real bug class (contract.rs's own module doc records two prior fidelity bugs where the recorder and the server silently diverged). `graph_wire.rs` is the DTO-identity layer: `encode_node_id`/`decode_node_id` are a proven bijection (graph_wire.rs:230-291 tests), and `parse_edge_kind` is total over `RelationId::ALL`/`SymRelationId::ALL` so a new relation can never go unparseable. atlas-cli reuses `atlas_server::graph_wire` and `atlas_server::handlers`/`graph_handlers` DTO field names directly (Cargo.toml's own R1 comment: "no parallel query logic"), so its JSON output is provably the same shape the HTTP API serves. Both crates are heavily test-covered: atlas-server's tests directory is larger than its src (12 files vs 11), spanning HTTP-level tests (api.rs, graph_api.rs), server-vs-model conformance (graph_conformance.rs, graph_equivalence.rs), a Gherkin-driven contract corpus (aqc_cucumber.rs) and a byte-for-byte regression pact (contract_pact.rs).

files.role: Workspace manifest — declares the five crates, plus a very long test-counting ritual
files.l1: This file is the master list of which Rust project folders belong to "the server" as one buildable unit — atlas-core, atlas-etl, atlas-server, atlas-graph, and atlas-cli. Nearly all of its length, though, is a running diary explaining a quirk: one more crate, graph-types, holds a lot of important tests but technically lives just outside this list (Cargo's rules won't let it be listed, since it sits one folder above). So whenever someone wants "how many tests pass right now," they can't just run one command — they have to run two and add the numbers together, and this file's giant header is where that two-step ritual and its running history are written down so nobody forgets it or miscounts.
files.l2: `[workspace] members = [...]` lists the five crates sharing one `Cargo.lock`. The header comment explains why `graph-types` (repo root) isn't in that list: **Cargo** requires every workspace member to live *underneath* the workspace root folder, and `graph-types/` is a sibling of `server/`, not a child of it — so it's pulled in only indirectly, as a path dependency of `atlas-graph`. The consequence is the "STANDING COUNTING PROCEDURE": a full test count is `cargo test --workspace` (everything reachable from this manifest) *plus* `cargo test -p atlas-graph-types` run separately (since `--workspace` alone never reaches a non-member crate), with every `"test result: ok. N passed"` line from both commands summed. The rest of the file is a long, append-only **ledger** — each development batch adds a paragraph recording the new total, which sections changed, and any test that failed for reasons unrelated to that batch's own code (a documented, disclosed judgment call, not a silent skip). This is a `Cargo-toml` concept: a `Cargo-toml` manifest can hold structured config (`[workspace]`, `resolver`) alongside plain `#`-comments that become load-bearing project history.
files.l3: `members = ["atlas-core", "atlas-etl", "atlas-server", "atlas-graph", "atlas-cli"]`, `resolver = "2"`. The STANDING COUNTING PROCEDURE (established at commit `f988f1b`) is restated by every batch: sum every `"test result: ok. N passed"` line from `cargo test --workspace` and `cargo test -p atlas-graph-types` run separately from `server/`, plus report the AQC corpus's own `scenarios/steps` count as a mandatory companion line (it never prints a `test result:` line at all, since `aqc_cucumber.rs` sets `harness = false` — see `atlas-server/Cargo.toml`). The ledger records the count moving from 747 (at `f988f1b`) through many batches to over 1050+ by the most recent entries read, each paragraph naming exactly which new test files/sections were added and disclosing any environment-sensitive timing-gate flake (e.g. `perf_smoke.rs`'s wall-clock thresholds, `graph_conformance.rs`'s 60s ceiling) rather than silently re-running until green. This is project culture made mechanical: a batch that cannot account for the exact delta in the total (old count + new tests − any newly-disclosed failure = new count) has not actually verified its own work. No test or build logic lives here beyond `[workspace]`/`resolver`; it purely declares crate membership and documents the counting discipline every other crate's CLAUDE-adjacent batch report must follow.

files.role: atlas-server's manifest — deps, its second export_aqc_examples binary, and its own test/bench targets
files.l1: This file lists what atlas-server needs to build (the web framework `axum`, the async runtime `tokio`, JSON support) and declares that this one project folder actually produces two separate runnable programs: the main server, and a small helper tool that regenerates the project's contract-testing examples. It also flags one of its test files as special (it runs its own way rather than the normal way) and registers a separate "benchmark" program for deep performance investigation.
files.l2: Standard `[package]`/`[dependencies]`/`[dev-dependencies]` sections. `default-run = "atlas-server"` disambiguates `cargo run -p atlas-server` now that a second `[[bin]]` (`export_aqc_examples`, at `src/bins/export_aqc_examples.rs` — deliberately outside `src/bin/` because this repo's `.gitignore` has a broad `**/bin/` rule for the Blazor client's build output) exists. `[[test]] name = "aqc_cucumber" harness = false` tells Cargo that `tests/aqc_cucumber.rs` is its own test runner (the `cucumber` crate's own `World::run`) rather than a normal `#[test]`-per-function binary — this is the `unit-test` vs `integration-test` distinction Rust's tooling draws, extended here by a third-party test harness. `[[bench]] name = "queries" harness = false` registers `benches/queries.rs` for `cargo bench`, using the `criterion` crate instead of Rust's built-in (and now-unstable) bench harness.
files.l3: Dependencies: `axum = "0.8"`, `tokio` (rt-multi-thread/macros/net features — the concrete `tokio` async runtime this crate actually drives, since `async-await` code needs an executor), `tower`/`tower-http` (cors, fs — used by `app.rs`'s SPA fallback and permissive CORS layer), `serde`/`serde_json`, `anyhow` (used in `main.rs`/`load.rs` for `Result`-with-context error plumbing). Dev-dependencies: `http-body-util` (test body extraction), `cucumber = "0.23"` + `futures` (the Gherkin harness, MIT/Apache-2.0, disclosed as a genuinely new test-time dependency), `criterion = "0.5"` (the bench harness). The comments trace two real build-tooling decisions to their originating batches (AQC-1 for the second `[[bin]]`/cucumber harness, PERF-2a for the criterion bench) rather than presenting them as defaults.

files.role: atlas-cli's manifest — depends on atlas-server itself to reuse its wire grammar, one [[bin]] named bibex
files.l1: This file lists what the command-line tool needs, and the interesting thing about it is that it depends on the WEB SERVER project too — not to run a server, but to reuse the server's own "how do we spell an id" and "how do we parse an edge kind" logic, so the command-line tool and the website never disagree about vocabulary. It also renames the actual program people run from the technical project name ("atlas-cli") to the friendlier "bibex" (Bible Explorer).
files.l2: `[dependencies]` includes `atlas-core`, `atlas-graph`, `atlas-graph-types` (the query engine and its types, same as atlas-server) plus `atlas-server = { path = "../atlas-server" }` — a library dependency reusing `atlas_server::graph_wire` (id encode/decode) and DTO field-name conventions, not a runtime dependency (this crate never starts a server or imports `axum`). `serde_json = "1"` supports `--json` mode, added as "a new edge in the dependency graph, not a new external crate" since it was already resolved workspace-wide. `[[bin]] name = "bibex" path = "src/main.rs"` is the rename: the crate is still called `atlas-cli` for Cargo's own bookkeeping, but the binary a user types is `bibex`.
files.l3: A removed-dependency note is preserved in comments: `anyhow` was declared but never imported (`load.rs` only calls `.map_err` on an already-typed `anyhow::Result`, never naming the `anyhow` type itself) — a dead dependency, caught in review and deleted ("FIX ROUND 1 (review T-1)"). The R1/R3 design rulings are restated here as comments: "no parallel query logic" (every graph question goes through `atlas_graph::GraphService`/`atlas_graph_types::store::GraphQuery`, or reuses `atlas-server`'s own id/edge-kind grammar as a library, never a hand-rolled duplicate) and "args hand-parsed... no clap, no new runtime deps beyond what atlas-server itself already brings in" (mirroring `atlas-server/src/main.rs`'s own hand-rolled flag loop rather than adding a CLI-argument-parsing crate).

files.role: The library root — declares atlas-server's modules so tests can call them directly
files.l1: This tiny file is the table of contents for the server's internal code. It exists so that the test files (which check the server's behavior) can reach directly into the server's logic — build the exact same web app the real server builds — without actually starting a real, listening server and making real network calls for every test.
files.l2: `pub mod app; pub mod aqc_export; pub mod contract; pub mod error; pub mod graph_handlers; pub mod graph_wire; pub mod handlers; pub mod load;` — this is Rust's `module` system: each line exposes one source file as a `module` other code (including `main.rs` and every file in `tests/`) can `use`. Because atlas-server is built as both a library (`lib.rs`) and a binary (`main.rs`), `main.rs` is described as "a thin binary shell... around `app::build`" — nearly all real logic lives in modules reachable from here, and `main.rs` just calls into them.
files.l3: The doc comment states the architectural reason directly: `tests/api.rs` and friends exercise `app::build` via `tower::ServiceExt::oneshot` (see `api.rs`, `graph_api.rs`), which requires `app` (and everything it touches) to be `pub` from a library target — a binary-only crate cannot be `use`d by an external test binary. `pub mod load` carries its own comment explaining CDC-1 fix round 1's motivation (the load path had to become the one shared assembly point after two provider/recorder-drift bugs — see `load.rs`). No logic of its own; purely a `module` re-export surface.

files.role: The atlas-server binary: parses CLI flags, loads data, starts listening
files.l1: This is the program that actually runs when someone starts the web server. It reads command-line options (which folder holds the compiled data, which network port to use), loads the graph either from a fast pre-built file or, for developers, freshly from raw source files, prints some helpful startup statistics, and then starts listening for web requests until the process is stopped.
files.l2: `parse_args` hand-parses `env::args()` into a small `Args` struct (`data_dir`, `static_dir`, `port`, `build_from_raw`) — no argument-parsing library, just a `while` loop over a `&[String]` `slice`. `#[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<()>` is the entry point: the `tokio` attribute macro sets up an async runtime so `main` itself can be `async fn` and use `.await`. The startup has two branches: the default path calls `atlas_server::load::load_graph_and_data`, which reads the pre-compiled `graph.bin` artifact (fast — a committed law keeps this under 3 seconds); `--build-from-raw` instead calls `atlas_etl::compile::compile` and `GraphService::build` to construct the graph in memory from raw source files (slower, for iterating on data without recompiling). Either way, the result is wrapped in `Arc` (an atomic reference-counted pointer — many async request handlers can each hold a cheap clone of the same graph without copying it) before being handed to `atlas_server::app::build_with_sources`. Finally `tokio::net::TcpListener::bind` opens the port and `axum::serve` runs forever, handling requests.
files.l3: `Args { data_dir: PathBuf, static_dir: Option<PathBuf>, port: u16, build_from_raw: bool }`; `parse_args(args: &[String]) -> Result<Args>` (anyhow::Result, using `.context(...)`/`bail!` for fail-loud, path-naming errors). `main` measures `load_start.elapsed()` and prints per-path stats (`graph.stats.kjv_verses`, `cites_rows`, event-world stats) so an operator can see load health at a glance. The doc comments record two real historical bugs this file's own structure now prevents: startup logic used to be hand-copied into the contract-pact test recorder and drifted from what the real binary did (fixed by extracting `atlas_server::load`, see load.rs); and a doubled word in a log format string ("artifact load load complete") was fixed by restructuring the format string rather than the branch strings. `sources` (the Sources-page registry) is loaded as a third, independent piece of state via `atlas_server::load::load_sources`, never folded into `AtlasData`. Wired to `graph_handlers`/`handlers` only indirectly, through `app::build_with_sources`.

files.role: The one function that turns a data_dir into a serving Router — shared by main.rs and the pact recorder
files.l1: This file exists because of a real mistake the project made twice: a test that regenerates "proof" of what the server does was accidentally built differently from the real server, so its proof was quietly wrong — once it claimed an entire page of data was there when it wasn't, and once it silently served nothing at all for a whole feature. The fix was to write the "load everything and get ready to serve" steps exactly once, in this file, so both the real server and the test that checks it are guaranteed to do the identical thing.
files.l2: `LoadedAtlas { data: Arc<AtlasData>, graph: Arc<GraphService>, sources: Arc<SourcesDocument> }` bundles the three pieces of server state into one `struct`, so "add a fourth ingredient" can't be done in only one of the two call sites. `load_sources` reads `sources.json` (fail-loud `Result` with `.context(...)` naming the exact path on failure — this is the `error-handling` idiom of returning a `Result<T, E>` and using the `?-operator` to propagate it up rather than a language-level exception). `load_graph_and_data` loads the compiled `graph.bin` artifact via `GraphService::from_artifact`, loads the remaining compiled JSON files via `AtlasData::load`, then rebuilds a few retiring fields directly from the graph (`atlas_graph::legacy::atlas_data_overlay`) before calling `.finish()` — the doc comment stresses this last `finish()` call is not optional: skipping it silently leaves derived lookups empty, which is exactly the second historical bug. `load_from_data_dir` composes both halves into one `LoadedAtlas`.
files.l3: `LoadedAtlas::into_router(self, static_dir) -> Router` is documented as "THE ONLY CALL SITE of `app::build_with_sources` outside tests that deliberately exercise a partial app" — a structural guarantee, not a convention, that the pact recorder and the production binary assemble the app identically. `load_graph_and_data(data_dir: &Path) -> Result<(GraphService, AtlasData)>` is called by both `main.rs`'s default branch and `tests/contract_pact.rs::app()`. Fix round 1 (review C-3) is the naming context: the recorder previously used `SourcesDocument::default()` (so `GET /api/sources` recorded empty against a real 18-source server) and ran the `--build-from-raw` path (so `AtlasData::finish()` never ran and `GET /api/catechism/{sref}` silently answered `[]` for every reference) — both green suites over wrong providers, the exact class of bug this module's existence prevents by removing the second copy entirely.

files.role: Router construction: maps every URL to its handler, wires shared state, layers CORS and the SPA fallback
files.l1: This file is the server's own map: it lists every web address the app understands (like `/api/verse/{vref}` or `/api/chapter/{cref}`) and says which piece of code answers each one. It also decides what happens when the address doesn't match any API route — instead of a plain error page, it serves the actual website files, so a browser bookmark to a specific page (like `/world`) still works.
files.l2: `AppState { data: Arc<AtlasData>, graph: Arc<GraphService>, sources: Arc<SourcesDocument> }` is a `#[derive(Clone)]` `struct` holding everything a handler might need. Each field gets an `impl FromRef<AppState> for Arc<T>` — this is `axum`'s way of letting a handler declare `State<Arc<GraphService>>` in its function signature and have axum automatically pull just that one field out of the combined `AppState`, without every handler needing to know about the other fields. `build_with_sources` constructs the `Router` with `.route(path, get(handler_fn))` for every endpoint, then (if a `static_dir` was given) attaches a fallback that serves the published website's files, rewriting a "file not found" 404 into a 200 so client-side page routes like `/world` don't look like errors to tools that check status codes. `CorsLayer::permissive()` is applied last, deliberately, so it wraps the static-file fallback too.
files.l3: 22 routes registered on one `api` sub-router built with `.with_state(state)`, then optionally wrapped with a `ServeDir::new(dir).not_found_service(ServeFile::new(index))` fallback (tower-http's documented single-page-app idiom) before `.layer(CorsLayer::permissive())`. The doc comment calls out a real fixed bug: `Router::layer` only wraps whatever exists on the router at call time, and `fallback_service` replaces the fallback with a brand-new `Route` that bypasses any layer applied earlier — so CORS must be layered *after* the fallback is attached, not before, or every SPA-served response would silently lack CORS headers while `/api/*` had them; `tests/api.rs::static_dir_serves_files_api_still_wins_and_falls_back_to_index_for_spa_routes` pins this ordering. `GraphService` is held concretely (not `Arc<dyn GraphQuery>`) because `GraphStore`'s associated-type shape (`type Snapshot: GraphSnapshot`) is not `dyn`-safe — the actual query surface every handler uses is still entirely the `GraphQuery` trait, opened via `graph.snapshot()`. `build(...)` is the pre-existing signature every non-sources test calls, delegating to `build_with_sources` with an empty `SourcesDocument::default()`.

files.role: The bulk of the HTTP API: one handler function plus wire DTOs per endpoint
files.l1: This is the biggest file in the server, and it's where most of the actual work happens: for each thing a browser can ask for — a Bible chapter, a single verse with everything attached to it, an event's details, a place's history, a catechism item, cross references — there is one function here that fetches the answer and shapes it into the exact JSON the client expects. It also carries the project's policy on tricky edge cases, like "what happens if someone asks for a chapter number that doesn't exist" (answer: an honest empty list, not an error) versus "what happens if someone asks for a verse that plain doesn't exist" (answer: a real 404).
files.l2: Every handler has the shape `pub async fn name(State(x): State<Arc<T>>, ...) -> Result<Json<Out>, ApiError>` — `axum`'s `extractor` pattern: `State<T>` pulls shared app state, `Path<String>` pulls a URL segment, `Query<HashMap<String,String>>` pulls query-string parameters. Dozens of `#[derive(Serialize)]` `struct`s (like `VerseDetailOut`, `EventDetailOut`, `ChapterOut`) are the actual JSON shapes; `serde`'s `#[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]` attribute is used everywhere to omit a field from the JSON entirely (rather than sending `null`) when there's genuinely nothing to say — the file's own convention is "never a silent blank and never a fabricated label." A recurring pattern is "provenance" fields: nearly every DTO carries a `String` or `Vec<String>` naming which real-world source (KJV, openbible.info, a hand-curated note) a piece of data came from, resolved via `snap.node(id).map(|n| n.provenance)` and failing loud (`ApiError::internal`) rather than defaulting if that attribution is ever missing. Two closely related sibling functions, `chapter` and `verse`, both read verse text through the SAME low-level `window::render` call the generic `/api/text` endpoint uses, so all three surfaces can never disagree about what a verse says.
files.l3: Notable handlers: `scene_time`/`scene_scripture` (time/scripture-window map scenes via `atlas_core::scene::compose_*`), `chapter` (handlers.rs:473, re-implemented over `GraphService::chapter_span` + `window::window`/`render`, proven byte-identical to the pre-migration lookup by `tests/graph_equivalence.rs`), `kretzmann_chapter` (handlers.rs:622, replaces a 176-request-per-chapter client fan-out with one server-side walk of `commented-on-by` edges), `verse` (handlers.rs:1006, assembles `VerseDetailOut` — text, events via the inverse `Attests` edge, cross-refs via `graph.cross_refs_by_from`, catechism citations, red-letter spans, and four separate provenance fields), `narrative_event_positions` (handlers.rs:1258, walks `Succession` edges tagged with `EdgeMeta::Narrative` via the private helper `drain_edges`, which pages through a whole edge frontier rather than one page), `event` (handlers.rs:1558) and `place` (handlers.rs:1968, the file's last handler, resolving `PlaceDetailOut` including a window-resolved historical name and an optional Easton's/Kretzmann `description`). `drain_edges` (handlers.rs:1370) is the one private helper reused by three handlers to fully page an edge frontier via `GraphQuery::edges`'s cursor. `CatechismRefOut`/`CrossRefOut::provenance` doc comments (handlers.rs:720-806) carry an extensive, self-correcting discussion of "section-level vs per-row" attribution granularity — a real design constraint (the underlying companion index doesn't carry per-row provenance) stated plainly after two earlier, wrong comments claimed otherwise, fixed across two review rounds. `ruling-3-policy` (referenced throughout) is the house rule for when an out-of-canon query is a 200-with-empty-result vs a 404/400.

files.role: The three generic, kind-agnostic graph endpoints: node card, node edges, text window
files.l1: Where handlers.rs has one bespoke function per specific feature (a verse, a place), this file has just three functions that work uniformly across EVERY kind of thing in the graph — any node, any relationship, any stretch of readable text. `GET /api/node/{id}` gives you a summary card for literally any node id; `GET /api/node/{id}/edges` walks any relationship from any node, one page at a time; `GET /api/text` reads a window of consecutive text (Bible verses, or paragraphs of Luther's Small Catechism) starting from a given reference. Together they're the general-purpose "explore anything" surface the other, more specific endpoints are built on top of.
files.l2: `node_card` (`GET /api/node/{id}`) decodes the wire id via `graph_wire::decode_node_id`, fetches the node with `snap.node(&node_id)`, and returns its label, provenance, and a summary of how many edges of each kind it has (`snap.edge_summary`). `node_edges` (`GET /api/node/{id}/edges?kind=&cursor=&limit=`) parses the `kind` string back into a strongly-typed `EdgeKind` via `graph_wire::parse_edge_kind`, then calls `snap.edges(position, &EdgeQuery { kind, cursor, limit })` — this is `GraphQuery`'s own cursor-based pagination primitive, capped between 1 and 200 entries per page (`.clamp(1, MAX_EDGE_LIMIT)`). `text_window` (`GET /api/text?ref=&n=&dir=&scope=&corpus=`) supports two corpora (`bible`, the default, and `concord`, the Book of Concord) and reads a window of text units via `window::window`/`window::render`, walking either `Onward` or `Backward` from a starting position — both are variants of a Rust `enum` called `WindowDir`. An HTTP `ETag`/`If-None-Match` check lets a client skip re-downloading text it already has, since the whole graph is immutable for the server's lifetime.
files.l3: `node_description` (graph_handlers.rs:98) is a small, deliberately-relocated helper (moved here from `atlas_graph::legacy` in a documented layering cleanup) matching on `NodePayload::{Place,Person,PeopleGroup,CommentaryItem}` to surface an optional Easton's/Kretzmann prose `description` — reused by both `node_card` and `handlers::place`. `node_edges` filters out any `PeopleGroup`-kind neighbor before returning it (graph_handlers.rs:234) because `graph_wire::decode_node_id` carries no `PeopleGroup` arm yet — a documented, disclosed, one-line-revertable serving-boundary projection (PG-1a), not a graph-level omission (the underlying `snap.edges` call is unfiltered). `parse_ref`/`parse_concord_ref` are the two ref grammars `text_window` accepts; `dir=backward` combined with `scope=chapter` is explicitly rejected (`ApiError::bad_dir`) as a parameter combination with no honest meaning, rather than silently misapplied — the doc comment for `text_window` (graph_handlers.rs:306) walks through a real historical bug this rejection replaces (a chapter-scoped backward window used to silently serve the PRECEDING chapter's tail). `DEFAULT_EDGE_LIMIT = 20`, `MAX_EDGE_LIMIT = 200` are the pagination constants.

files.role: The id/edge-kind encoding layer between the graph's internal ids and human-readable wire strings
files.l1: The graph keeps track of things using its own internal id format, but a web address or a JSON field needs a readable string like `"Event:ab_ur"` or `"text-unit:JHN.3.16"`. This file is the translator in both directions: given an internal id, produce the readable string a client should see; given a readable string a client sent back, resolve it to the internal id. It also translates relationship names — a caller says `"cites"` or `"located-at"`, and this file turns that into the internal, strongly-typed representation the graph actually understands.
files.l2: `encode_node_id(id: &AnyNodeId) -> String` `match`es on the node's `kind` (an `enum`): a `TextUnit` becomes `"text-unit:JHN.3.16"` (via `atlas_graph::kjv_adapter`) or a Book-of-Concord citation string; every other kind falls through to a generic `"{Kind:?}:{raw}"` format (using Rust's `Debug-Display` `{:?}` formatting on the `enum` variant). `decode_node_id(s: &str) -> Option<AnyNodeId>` is the inverse, `match`ing on the string's `"kind:"` prefix — returning `Option::None` (not panicking) for anything unrecognized, so a bad id from a client becomes an honest 400, never a crash. `parse_edge_kind(label: &str) -> Option<EdgeKind>` is described as a "total inverse" of a relation's own `.label()` method, built by looping over `RelationId::ALL`/`SymRelationId::ALL` — an array `const`ant graph-types declares — rather than a hand-written table, so a newly added relation is automatically parseable here with zero code change.
files.l3: The module doc comment frames the whole file as "wire-identity conversions... kept entirely at this DTO layer" — graph-types' own `AnyNodeId`/`EdgeKind` are untouched; this is purely a presentation-layer bijection. Each node kind this graph has ever grown (`Event`, `Narrative`, `Anchor`, `Place`, `Era`, `Polity`, `CatechismItem`, `Person`, `Translation`, `CommentaryItem`, `Container`) got exactly one new `match` arm added to `decode_node_id` in its own historical batch, because `encode_node_id`'s generic fallback already produced the matching wire string for free — the file's own test `event_narrative_anchor_place_ids_round_trips_through_the_wire_form` (graph_wire.rs:235) proves every one of those 13+ kind/id pairs round-trips exactly. `describe_node`/`describe_position` (graph_wire.rs:187, 220) produce a human label for any `Position` (node or edge) by falling back to graph-types' own `card()` view assembly rather than re-deriving a label match locally. This file is the SAME grammar `atlas-cli` reuses directly (`use atlas_server::graph_wire::{decode_node_id, describe_node, ...}`) rather than reimplementing — the concrete mechanism behind the "one source of truth for id spelling" design rule stated in atlas-cli's Cargo.toml.

files.role: ApiError — the one error type every handler returns, rendered as {"error":{"code","message"}}
files.l1: Every question this server can fail to answer fails the same way: a matching HTTP status code and a small JSON object naming what went wrong and why. This file is where that one shape is defined, along with a labeled constructor for each kind of failure — a bad reference, something not found, a bad request parameter, or an internal problem — so every part of the server reports errors consistently instead of each handler inventing its own error format.
files.l2: `ApiError { status: StatusCode, code: &'static str, message: String }` is one plain `struct`, not an `enum` of error variants — a deliberate simplicity choice. Named constructor functions (`bad_window`, `bad_ref`, `not_found`, `bad_kind`, `bad_dir`, `bad_corpus`, `internal`) each fix a status code and a fixed `code` string, so the same failure always looks the same on the wire. `impl IntoResponse for ApiError` is the `trait` `axum` calls automatically whenever a handler's `Result<_, ApiError>` is `Err` — this is why a handler can just `return Err(ApiError::not_found("verse"))` and axum handles turning that into an actual HTTP response.
files.l3: The module doc comment states a controller ruling explicitly: axum's own default extractor-rejection body must never reach the client, so every handler deliberately uses lenient extractors (`Query<HashMap<String,String>>` rather than a strongly-typed `Query<T>`, plain `Path<String>`) that cannot themselves fail to deserialize, converting every "missing/unparseable/out of shape" case into one of these typed errors instead. `ApiError::internal` (error.rs:85) is the newest constructor, added for exactly one class of failure the server-side fail-loud law creates: a node whose text rendered successfully but which carries no provenance string to attribute it to — a 500 naming the id, deliberately distinct from `not_found` ("the resource DOES exist; this project's own data about it is incomplete, which is our bug, not the caller's").

files.role: Pure (no I/O) generation logic for the AQC contract's Gherkin feature files and fixture list
files.l1: The project's automated contract tests are written in a plain-English-like format (Gherkin), and rather than someone hand-typing every example in those files, this file generates them from a fixed list of real ids in the real graph. Keeping the actual file-writing separate from this generation logic means a second, standing test can call the exact same generation functions and check that the committed files still match — so nobody can hand-edit the generated files and have that drift go unnoticed.
files.l2: Three `pub const` arrays are the actual data: `SEEDS` (one real node id per kind the graph carries, e.g. `("Event", "Event:ab_ur")`), `FOCUS_IDENTITY_EXTRA` (one extra round-trip case), and `FIXTURES` (a list of `(name, url)` pairs for HTTP responses to capture, including deliberately bad requests like a malformed id, to prove error paths too). `path_encode` percent-encodes the one wire character (`/`) that would otherwise collide with URL routing. `focus_query_feature()`/`exploration_roundtrip_feature()` are plain functions returning `String`s of Gherkin text, built with Rust's `format!` macro — no template engine, just string formatting.
files.l3: The doc comment explains the extraction: this pure logic used to live only in `src/bins/export_aqc_examples.rs`; it was factored out in "fix round 1 (Q-6)" specifically so `tests/aqc_corpus_generation.rs` can call `focus_query_feature()`/`exploration_roundtrip_feature()` directly and byte-compare their output against the committed `.feature` files, catching drift without needing to run the binary or touch the real graph. Every `SEEDS` id is documented as independently verified live against the real graph by the exporter binary at generation time (never invented) and deliberately excludes the KJV translation (`brainfuel_layers.rs::no_kjv_translation_node_is_authored_this_batch` proves KJV is the canonical layer itself, not a Translation node). `examples_table` right-pads a Gherkin `Examples:` table by computing the widest kind/id string first — a small, self-contained column-alignment routine.

files.role: The second binary: builds the real graph, verifies every seed id, writes .feature files and fixture JSON to disk
files.l1: This is a small standalone tool (run by hand, not part of normal server startup) that regenerates the project's contract-test example files. It builds the real graph from scratch, double-checks that every example id it's about to use actually still exists (so a renamed or deleted record fails loudly here rather than shipping a broken example), and then writes out both the Gherkin feature files and a set of captured real HTTP responses other test suites read as fixtures.
files.l2: `#[tokio::main] async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()>` compiles the graph via `atlas_etl::compile::compile` and `GraphService::build`, then loops over `aqc_export::SEEDS`, asserting each seed id both round-trips (`decode_node_id` then `encode_node_id` gives back the same string) and resolves against the real graph (`snap.node(&decoded)`) — using `panic!` deliberately on failure, since this is a maintenance tool where "fail loud immediately" is exactly right. `capture(app, uri)` makes one in-process HTTP request via `tower::ServiceExt::oneshot` (no real network socket) and returns `{"status": ..., "body": ...}` as a `serde_json::Value`. The final loop writes one JSON fixture file per seed and per `FIXTURES` entry, plus an `index.json` mapping every wire id used to its fixture name.
files.l3: Located deliberately outside `src/bin/` — the repo's own root `.gitignore` has a broad `**/bin/` rule intended for the Blazor client's .NET build output, so this source lives at `src/bins/export_aqc_examples.rs` and is registered explicitly via the `[[bin]]` table in `Cargo.toml`, the same disclosed workaround `atlas-graph`'s `compile_graph.rs` and `atlas-etl`'s `gen_sources.rs` use. `identity_index` (a `BTreeMap<String,String>`) is keyed by the REQUEST id, never the response's own echoed id — this distinction matters because it's what lets a consuming test's round-trip proof genuinely fail if the bijection ever breaks, rather than trivially passing by comparing a value to itself. Run via `cargo run -p atlas-server --bin export_aqc_examples` from `server/`.

files.role: Proves the server's in-memory graph store answers every question exactly like the raw built model, over real KJV text
files.l1: The graph engine defines a strict promise (a trait/interface) about how it will answer questions, and this test is the proof that atlas-server's actual storage keeps that promise for real Bible text — not just that the code compiles against the interface. It runs the check twice: once on a small, real four-chapter slice (the Book of Ruth) for speed, and once, more slowly, on the entire real 31,102-verse Bible plus every event, place, and relationship the graph carries.
files.l2: `assert_answers_match(&snapshot, &model)` is the actual conformance law (owned by graph-types, called here, not modified) — it compares every node/edge/reading-window answer the candidate (a published, opened `MemStore` snapshot, the exact kind of handle the real server holds) gives against the model (the raw, freshly-built `Graph`), panicking with a precisely named divergence at the first mismatch. The Ruth-slice test slices the real `data/raw/kjv.json` down to one book via `serde_json::Value` manipulation rather than hand-typing test data, so every byte compared is real KJV text, just fewer verses of it.

files.role: Byte-identity regression harness: pins hashes of 25 real scene responses so a silent behavior change fails loud
files.l1: Two of the most-used endpoints — the time-window scene and the scripture-window scene — get their exact output fingerprinted here for 25 real, representative requests. If a future change ever silently alters what one of those requests returns, this test fails immediately by hash mismatch, without the project needing to store the (large) actual responses.
files.l2: Each test case computes a real scene response, hashes it with FNV-1a (a small, fixed, dependency-free hashing algorithm chosen specifically because Rust's built-in `DefaultHasher` is NOT guaranteed stable across compiler versions — using it here would eventually cause false-positive failures unrelated to any real change), and compares against a hard-coded expected hash. The file frames this explicitly as "commit the harness, not the captured fixtures" — a single response can be ~205KB, so hashing avoids committing several megabytes of JSON for no real benefit.
files.l3: The module doc comment is itself a running ledger (much like server/Cargo.toml's) recording exactly which batches legitimately moved these hashes and why (a data batch merging duplicate events, a container-node batch, etc.) versus batches that made zero changes here and are expected to see the hashes hold steady as proof of "zero behavior change." This is not a security property — a scene response is public data — the value being bought is a cheap, algorithmically-stable fingerprint, nothing more.

files.role: CliError — the one error type every command returns, with a fixed 5-class taxonomy and matching exit codes
files.l1: Whenever bibex can't answer a question, it fails in one of exactly five well-defined ways (a typo in the command, a badly-formed reference, a real-looking id that doesn't exist, missing data files, or a real question with zero results) — and each of those five ways always prints the same shaped message and exits with the same fixed numeric code, so a script calling bibex can reliably tell what went wrong just from the exit code.
files.l2: `CliError` is a Rust `enum` with five variants (`BadUsage`, `BadRef`, `NotFound`, `DataLoadFailed`, `EmptyResult`), each carrying the same three `String` fields (`what`, `why`, `do_`). `code()` and `exit_code()` are `match` statements mapping each variant to its fixed label and integer. `impl fmt::Display for CliError` renders the plain-text form (`"atlas: error (<code>): <what> -- <why> -- <what to do>"`); `to_json()` renders the exact same three fields as a `{"error":{"code","message","hint"}}` JSON object for `--json` mode — one source of truth, two renderings, so the two output modes can never disagree about what an error means.
files.l3: `exit_code()` (error.rs:60) fixes: `EmptyResult` = 1, `BadRef` = 2, `NotFound` = 3, `BadUsage` = 4, `DataLoadFailed` = 5 — a documented, stable contract (`CONTRACT.md`'s own error taxonomy table) that `tests/cli.rs` asserts directly for every class. `parts()` (error.rs:70) is a private helper using Rust's `|`-pattern (matching several enum variants in one arm, since all five share the same field shape) to extract `(what, why, do_)` once, reused by both `Display` and `to_json` so the two renderings can never drift on which text goes where.

files.role: bibex verse <ref> — one verse's text, red-letter marks, and every attached place/person/event/passage
files.l1: This is the single-verse deep-dive command: given a reference like `GEN.1.1`, it prints that verse's text with Christ's words bracketed, then lists every place, person, event, and general passage the graph knows is connected to that exact verse — each with its own id right there in brackets, ready to look up further with `bibex node`.
files.l2: `resolve_kjv` gathers the verse text (`window::render`), its red-letter spans, and its attached places/persons/events (split into `events` and `passages` by the underlying `Event::kind` field, so a real dated event and a general literary passage like a Psalm's acrostic stanza never get lumped together). `mark_red_letter(text, spans)` walks the text left-to-right once, wrapping each non-overlapping span in `[...]` brackets — a small, self-contained string-building function, separately unit tested. The function also handles the Book of Concord case (a leaner, untracked shape) via the same `decode_node_id`-based dispatch `chapter.rs`/`graph_wire.rs` establish.
files.l3: `attached(kind, raw, label)` and the `Attached { id, label }` struct are the concrete mechanism behind the BIBEX-1 addendum's "IDS EVERYWHERE" ruling — every displayed name is always paired with its exact `graph_wire::encode_node_id`-produced id, so a user can always copy an id straight out of `bibex verse`'s output into `bibex node`. `events`/`passages` being separate fields (not one list with a flag) directly encodes the owner's PERI-1 ruling ("NUN is not an event") at the command layer, exactly mirroring `atlas_server::handlers::VerseEventOut.kind`'s server-side distinction. `pub(crate) fn mark_red_letter` is reused by `chapter.rs`.

files.role: The CLI's own fragment of the cross-transport consumer-driven contract pact
files.l1: Since bibex answers many of the same questions the web server does, this file makes sure they actually AGREE — it runs the same set of questions from the Gherkin contract files through the real bibex binary and records the answers, the CLI's own contribution to a combined pact file both transports (HTTP and CLI) are checked against together.
files.l2: `cli_keys()` reads the list of bibex invocations the Gherkin corpus asks for — but crucially does NOT re-derive that list itself; it reads it from `contracts/pacts/http.json`, already published by the HTTP recorder (`atlas-server/tests/contract_pact.rs`). This avoids two independent parsers of the same Gherkin files potentially disagreeing about what a step line means — one rule lives in one place.
files.l3: The module doc comment explains a genuine cross-crate constraint: `env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_bibex")` is only defined for tests belonging to the package that declares that binary (atlas-cli), so this recorder cannot live inside atlas-server's own test suite even though the two conceptually belong together — "one recorder per crate that OWNS a transport is the smaller rule." A documented ordering dependency follows directly from this design: adding a new bibex step to a feature file requires re-running the HTTP recorder FIRST (to refresh `cli_keys` in `http.json`), then this one — and if forgotten, the shared contract runner fails loudly by naming the missing pact entry rather than silently passing.
